request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Final Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a moderate traumatic brain injury, stigmas of trauma in the anterior chest wall, and signs of respiratory distress after falling off a cliff while riding his bicycle. Upon admission, a thoracoabdominal computed tomography angiography reported pneumomediastinum, a small right pneumothorax, and an image of loss of continuity in the anterior superior wall of the right main bronchus highly suggestive of bronchial rupture. The bronchial lesion was confirmed by fiberoptic bronchoscopy, showing a linear 1-cm rupture at the level of the root of the right main bronchus, in its lateral aspect, with fracture of the entire bronchial wall. Conservative management was chosen, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) with protective tracheal intubation. The patient’s ICU stay included a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute, tidal volume of 6–8 ml/kg, I/E 1:3, PEEP 5 cm H2O, and plateau pressure of < 30 mmHg. After 48 hours, the pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum resolved spontaneously, with limited subcutaneous emphysema, and the patient was successfully extubated on day 4. Strict follow-up was performed without evidence of swallowing or respiratory disorders, which allowed for the patient’s discharge 1 week later.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient is considered stable with no evidence of respiratory or swallowing disorders.

Follow-Up Plans:
Patient will follow-up in 4-6 weeks for scheduled evaluation.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: S27**

The principal diagnosis is the traumatic rupture of the right main bronchus, which falls under S27 (Injury of other and unspecified intrathoracic organs; S27.5 is injury of bronchus). The hospital course centres on this injury: confirmation by bronchoscopy, conservative management, ICU transfer and ventilation, and management of the resulting pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum. The traumatic brain injury is also an injury, but the course does not focus on its treatment, so it is coded as a additional diagnosis rather than the principal one.
